2.subtitle: Before the code, see why this one idea shows up in nearly every app you use.

parts.title: The Big Idea
parts.video_title: Watch: Why Learn OOP in Python?
parts.quote: Object-oriented programming is more than a technique. It is a way of thinking about problems and building software that can grow with confidence.
parts.prompt: Name an app you use daily. What objects could it contain?
parts.placeholder: e.g. Banking app → Account, Transaction, User…

cards.title: Industry Standard
cards.text: OOP drives enterprise software, games, web apps and AI. Learn it once and it opens doors almost everywhere.

cards.title: Python Is Everywhere
cards.text: From Django web apps to AI models, Python's object features sit at the core of the tools you'll use.

cards.title: Think Like an Engineer
cards.text: Modeling problems as objects keeps big systems modular, reusable and easier to fix.

parts.title: Meet Your First Object
parts.concept: Every character in a game is an **object**: it has data (a name) and behaviors (greeting). A **class** is the blueprint that stamps them out.
parts.footnote: Don't worry about the syntax yet. Topic 1 explains each piece.

sandbox.task: Games model every player as an object. Give this Player a name (replace the ___) and run it to hear it greet you.
sandbox.hint: Any name works, e.g. Player("Juan"). Keep the quotes.

3.subtitle: Here's the plan for Object-Oriented Programming in Python: what you'll learn, in what order, and what you need.

parts.title: What You'll Be Able to Do
parts.intro: By the end of this module, you will be able to:

outcomes.text: Explain the basic OOP concepts: class, object, property and method.
Reuse code by building child classes that inherit from a parent using super().
Protect data with private attributes, @property getters and setters.
Apply polymorphism so different classes respond to the same method.

parts.check_task: Tick each item off to get set up.
checks: A device with internet (the code editor is built in)
Basic Python: variables, loops and functions
About 2 hours of focused study time
A notebook for sketching class diagrams (optional)

cards.title: Introduction to OOP
cards.text: Paradigms, class, object, property and method.

parts.title: Warm-up: Test Your Editor
parts.concept: Every concept in this module has a **Try it yourself** editor. Write Python, press **Run**, and the app checks your output instantly. Nothing to install.
parts.analogy: Mistakes are part of coding. Error messages are clues, not failures.

sandbox.task: Quick test of the built-in editor: make Python greet the module by printing Hello, ITiKODE!
sandbox.hint: Replace the three underscores with ITiKODE.

4.subtitle: Meet the big idea: programs built from objects that mirror the real world.

parts.title: Programming Paradigms

round.task: Find the matching cards, then type the right words over the blanks so each language prints its style.
round.hint: Procedural is a recipe of steps. Functional chains functions. Object-oriented models real-world things.

pairs.clue: A real thing made from a class
Language that can do all three

parts.concept: A **paradigm** is a style of writing software. **Procedural** code is a recipe of steps, **functional** code chains math-like functions, and **object-oriented** code models real-world things as objects. Python lets you use all three.
parts.analogy: Procedural = a baking recipe. OOP = a kitchen full of tools that know how to do their own jobs.
parts.example:
# Procedural: steps, top to bottom
print("Step 1: Mix flour and eggs")
print("Step 2: Pour into a pan")

sandbox.task: Finish the recipe! Add a third step that tells us to bake the cake for 30 minutes.
sandbox.starter:
# Procedural style: a list of steps
print("Step 1: Mix flour and eggs")
print("Step 2: Pour into a pan")
# TODO: print "Step 3: Bake for 30 minutes"
sandbox.solution:
print("Step 1: Mix flour and eggs")
print("Step 2: Pour into a pan")
print("Step 3: Bake for 30 minutes")
sandbox.hint: Use print() with a string that starts with "Step 3:".

parts.title: Class: The Blueprint

round.task: Fill the blanks to build the Student class. The last line should print the class name.
round.solution:
class Student:
    pass

kid = Student()
print(type(kid).__name__)
round.hint: A class starts with the class keyword and a CapitalizedName. An empty body needs pass.

pairs.clue: Tells you what kind an object is

parts.concept: A **class** is a blueprint used to create objects. It defines the properties and methods that every object made from it will have. In Python you declare one with the `class` keyword.
parts.analogy: A house blueprint isn't a house. It's the plan you can build many houses from.

sandbox.task: Name the class Student by replacing the blank, then run it. We build one object from it to prove it works.
sandbox.solution:
class Student:
    pass

kid = Student()
print(type(kid).__name__)
sandbox.hint: Replace ___ with the class name: Student (no quotes).

parts.title: Object: A Real Instance

round.task: Fill the blanks so Maria and Alex are created and every object is printed.
round.starter:
class Student:
    def ___(self, name):
        self.name = name

juan = Student("Juan")
maria = ___
alex = ___

___ s in [juan, maria, alex]:
    print("Object:", s.name)
round.hint: Calling the class like a function creates an object: Student("Maria").

pairs.clue: Goes through a list one by one

parts.concept: An **object** is an instance of a class: a real entity stamped out from the blueprint. Calling the class like a function creates one. `__init__` runs automatically and sets the object up.
parts.analogy: Juan, Maria and Alex are three different BSIT students, all built from the same Student blueprint.

sandbox.task: Create two more Student objects: maria and alex. The loop prints every one of them.
sandbox.hint: Same pattern as juan: Student("Maria") and Student("Alex").

parts.title: Property: What an Object Knows

round.task: Fill the blanks so the age is saved as a property and the last line prints it.
round.hint: Properties are attached to self inside __init__: self.age = age.

parts.concept: **Properties** (also called attributes) are variables that store information about an object, such as `name`, `age` or `gender`. Inside a class, attach them to `self`.
parts.analogy: A student ID card: name, age, course. These are the details the object carries around.

sandbox.task: The constructor receives an age but never stores it. Save it as a property so the last line works.
sandbox.hint: Mirror the line above it: self.age = age

parts.title: Method: What an Object Does

round.task: Fill the blanks to add take_exam() and call both methods on Maria.
round.hint: Define a method with def. Its first parameter is always self.

parts.concept: **Methods** are functions defined inside a class. They describe the behaviors of an object, like `study()`, `take_exam()` or `submit_project()`. The first parameter is always `self`.
parts.analogy: If properties are nouns on the ID card, methods are the verbs: study, take an exam, submit.

sandbox.task: Add a take_exam() method that prints "<name> is taking the exam". Both calls at the bottom should work.
sandbox.hint: Copy the shape of study(): def take_exam(self): then a print using self.name.

6.subtitle: Let a child class reuse, extend and reshape what its parent already does.

parts.title: Parent and Child Classes

round.task: Fill the blanks so Dog inherits from Animal and rex can eat.
round.hint: Put the parent name in parentheses: class Dog(Animal):

pairs.clue: A child gets the parent's members

parts.concept: **Inheritance** lets a child class acquire the attributes and methods of a parent class. It models an *is-a* relationship: a Dog **is an** Animal. Put the parent's name in parentheses to inherit.
parts.analogy: You inherit your surname and some traits from your parents without having to write them yourself.

sandbox.task: Make Dog inherit from Animal. Then rex can eat() without Dog defining it.
sandbox.hint: Put the parent class name inside the parentheses.

parts.title: Extending the Parent

round.task: Fill the blanks so Dog has its own bark() that prints Woof! and rex can eat and bark.
round.hint: A child can add new methods. Dog gets bark(); eat() still comes from Animal.

pairs.clue: A new method only Dog has
The object itself, in a method

parts.concept: A child keeps everything from its parent **and** can add brand-new members of its own. That's how a specific class grows on top of a general one.
parts.analogy: All animals eat, but only dogs bark. The child adds the skill the parent never had.

sandbox.task: Give Dog its own bark() method that prints Woof! so rex can eat and bark.
sandbox.hint: Replace pass with def bark(self): and a print("Woof!") line indented under it.

parts.title: Calling the Parent with super()

round.task: Fill the blanks so the parent constructor saves the name, then both values print.
round.hint: super().__init__(name) runs the parent setup first.

pairs.clue: Reaches the parent from the child

parts.concept: When a child has its own `__init__`, the parent's constructor is skipped unless you call it. `super().__init__(...)` runs the parent's setup first, then you add the child-only attributes.
parts.analogy: Before a new student sets up a course schedule, the school first records their basic person details.

sandbox.task: Call the parent constructor so name gets saved, then run to see both values.

parts.title: Method Overriding

round.task: Fill the blanks so Parrot overrides sound() and returns Hello!.
round.hint: Use the same method name in the child. Python picks the child version first.

pairs.clue: Method name shared by all birds

parts.concept: A child can **override** a parent method by defining one with the same name. Python always picks the child's version first, and falls back to the parent's if there isn't one.
parts.analogy: Every bird makes *some* noise. A parrot replaces the generic noise with a word.

sandbox.task: Override sound() in Parrot so it returns "Hello!". Bird and Crow should stay as they are.
sandbox.hint: Define def sound(self): inside Parrot and return the string.

8.subtitle: Bundle data with behavior and guard it behind a clean public interface.

parts.title: Public, Protected, Private

round.task: Fill the blanks so the private PIN is read through a method inside the class.
round.starter:
class Phone:
    def __init__(self):
        self.model = "ITi-X"
        self._battery = 80
        self.___ = "1234"

    def get_pin(self):
        ___ self.__pin

p = Phone()
print(p.model)
print(p._battery)
print(p.___())
round.solution:
class Phone:
    def __init__(self):
        self.model = "ITi-X"
        self._battery = 80
        self.__pin = "1234"

    def get_pin(self):
        return self.__pin

p = Phone()
print(p.model)
print(p._battery)
print(p.get_pin())
round.hint: Private names start with two underscores. A method inside the class can still return it.

pairs.clue: Safe way to read the PIN

parts.concept: Python marks access by naming. `attr` is **public**, `_attr` is **protected** (a polite “internal use” convention) and `__attr` is **private**, name-mangled so it can't be reached directly from outside.
parts.analogy: A phone's model is visible to all, battery health is for the owner, and the PIN stays locked.

sandbox.task: The last line crashes because __pin is private. Add a get_pin() method inside Phone and print the PIN through it.
sandbox.starter:
class Phone:
    def __init__(self):
        self.model = "ITi-X"
        self._battery = 80
        self.__pin = "1234"

    # add get_pin() here

p = Phone()
print(p.model)
print(p._battery)
print(p.__pin)   # ❌ crashes, fix me
sandbox.solution:
class Phone:
    def __init__(self):
        self.model = "ITi-X"
        self._battery = 80
        self.__pin = "1234"

    def get_pin(self):
        return self.__pin

p = Phone()
print(p.model)
print(p._battery)
print(p.get_pin())
sandbox.hint: Inside the class, self.__pin works. Return it from get_pin(), then call p.get_pin().

parts.title: Validating Before Changing

round.task: Fill the blanks so only positive deposits are accepted. The -20 must be ignored.
round.hint: Check first: if amount > 0 then add it.

parts.concept: The point of hiding data is control. Instead of letting anyone overwrite a value, expose a **method** that checks the new value first. Bad input is rejected and the object stays valid.
parts.analogy: A bank teller checks every deposit slip instead of letting you reach into the vault.

sandbox.task: Only accept positive deposits. Replace the blank so that the -20 is ignored.
sandbox.hint: The blank is the keyword if.

parts.title: The @property Decorator

round.task: Fill the blanks so c.diameter works like an attribute and prints 10.
round.hint: Put @property above the method. The diameter is the radius times 2.

pairs.clue: Makes a method act like data

parts.concept: `@property` turns a method into a read-only attribute. Callers write `c.diameter` instead of `c.diameter()`, yet the value is still computed safely inside the class.
parts.analogy: A car's speedometer: you just read the number, you don't ask the engine to compute it.

sandbox.task: Right now print(c.diameter) shows a method object. Add the decorator so it prints 10.
sandbox.hint: Write @property on the line directly above def diameter.

parts.title: Property Setters with Rules

round.task: Fill the blanks so the grade setter only accepts values from 0 to 100.
round.hint: Use @grade.setter, then check 0 <= value <= 100, otherwise print the message.

parts.concept: Pair `@property` with `@name.setter` to allow writing, but only through your rules. `s.grade = 95` looks like plain assignment, yet your validation runs behind the scenes.
parts.analogy: A thermostat accepts any dial turn, but caps it at the machine's safe range.

sandbox.task: The setter accepts anything. Add a check: if value is between 0 and 100 save it, otherwise print Invalid grade!
sandbox.hint: if 0 <= value <= 100: save it, else: print("Invalid grade!")

10.subtitle: One method name, many forms. Write code that works on anything that fits.

parts.title: One Name, Many Forms

round.task: Fill the blanks to add a Cow class whose speak() returns Moo.
round.hint: Every animal has the same method name, speak, but its own answer.

parts.concept: **Polymorphism** means “many forms”. Different classes can define the same method name, and each one responds in its own way. The caller doesn't need to care which object it holds.
parts.analogy: Say “speak!” to a dog, a cat and a cow. Same command, three different sounds.

sandbox.task: Add a Cow class whose speak() returns "Moo". The loop is already waiting for it.
sandbox.hint: class Cow: then def speak(self): return "Moo"

parts.title: A Shared Interface

round.task: Fill the blanks so Triangle overrides area() with half of base times height.
round.hint: The area of a triangle is 0.5 * base * height.

parts.concept: Child classes can all override a parent's method, giving a family of objects one **common interface**. One loop can then treat squares, circles and triangles alike.
parts.analogy: A teacher asks every shape “what's your area?” and each knows its own formula.

sandbox.task: Triangle forgot its own area(). Override it: half of base times height.

parts.title: Duck Typing

round.task: Fill the blanks so Rock can quack too and the loop works.
round.hint: Duck typing only needs the method to exist. Give Rock a quack() that prints "...".

pairs.clue: Error when the method is missing
A class with no quack yet
Judge an object by its methods

parts.concept: Python doesn't check *what* an object is, only whether it has the method you call. “If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck...” Unrelated classes work in the same function.
parts.analogy: A USB port doesn't care if it's a fan or a keyboard, as long as it fits the plug.
parts.example:
def make_it_quack(thing):
    thing.quack()   # any object will do

sandbox.task: Rock has no quack(), so the loop crashes. Teach it to quack by printing "...".
sandbox.hint: Replace pass with def quack(self): print("...")

parts.title: Polymorphism in Built-ins

round.task: Fill the blanks so printing a Pet shows Pet: Milo.
round.hint: Define __str__ to control how print() shows your object.

pairs.clue: Controls how print shows an object

parts.concept: You use polymorphism every day. `len()` works on strings, lists and dicts, and `print()` asks each object for its text through `__str__`. Define `__str__` to control how your own objects look.
parts.analogy: A universal remote works on every TV because each brand answers the same buttons.

sandbox.task: Define __str__ so print(Pet("Milo")) shows Pet: Milo.
